source: Wikipedia: Candle problem (Duncker 1935/1945; Glucksberg 1962)
finding: Duncker's candle task: fix a candle to a wall using a candle, matches and a box of tacks. The box must become a shelf. Glucksberg (1962) tested whether filling the box makes the task harder.
numbers: Glucksberg 2x2 design: tacks/matches inside vs outside their boxes, with or without cash prizes ($5 / $20). Empty-box condition: more solvers and faster. Filled-box condition: high-drive subjects did worse than low-drive. No N or percentages on the page.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Page dates Duncker 1935 (German book) while English monograph is 1945. Drive explanation disputed: no main effect of drive.
agent_relevance: Fixation is a property of how the problem is presented, not only of the solver. The same task changes difficulty with how objects are named and shown.

source: Wikipedia: Candle problem (presentation manipulations; Frank and Ramscar, Higgins and Chaires)
finding: Wording and layout change fixation. Underlining the relevant nouns helps. Piling tacks beside the box (not in it) makes nearly everyone solve it.
numbers: Frank and Ramscar written version at Stanford: underlining relevant materials raised solvers from 25% to 50%. Higgins and Chaires: 'box and tacks' beats 'box of tacks'. Tacks beside box: virtually all reach the optimal solution.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Percentages differ slightly from the functional-fixedness page (23% to 55%). Sample sizes not given.
agent_relevance: O6 lever: restate the problem with the object named as a bare part ('box', not 'box of tacks'). Wording of the restatement is a measurable lever.

source: Wikipedia: Functional fixedness (Adamson 1952 replication of Duncker)
finding: Adamson (1952) repeated Duncker's box experiment with a pre-utilization group (box filled with tacks) and a no-pre-utilization group (empty box).
numbers: Participants given the empty box were about twice as likely to solve it. No N or statistics on the page.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Adamson reported a 'repetition of three experiments'. Exact counts need the 1952 J. Exp. Psych. 44:288-291 paper.
agent_relevance: Replicates the founding effect: prior use of an object as a container blocks use as a support. Baseline effect is roughly a factor of two in solve rate.

source: Wikipedia: Functional fixedness (Frank and Ramscar 2003 written candle problem)
finding: Written candle problem, Stanford undergraduates. Underlining noun phrases reduces fixation.
numbers: Plain Duncker wording: 23% solved. Noun phrases underlined (e.g. 'box of matches'): 55%. Only the noun 'box' underlined: 47%. Follow-up underlining all nouns except 'box' gave similar results. No N on the page.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Gives 23/55 where the candle page gives 25/50. Treat as about 25% to 50%.
agent_relevance: The solve rate at baseline is low (about a quarter) even for educated adults. A cheap surface cue can double it.

source: Wikipedia: Functional fixedness (Maier 1930/31; Birch and Rabinowitz 1951)
finding: Two-cord problem: the solver must see a heavy object as a pendulum weight. Birch and Rabinowitz showed that earlier use of an object in one function blocks its use in another.
numbers: Three groups: relay pretest (R), switch pretest (S), control (C, engineering students). C used both objects about equally as pendulum weight. R used the switch almost exclusively. Most of S used the relay. No N on the page.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Effect is directional: the object not used in pretraining is chosen. It is a set effect as well as a fixedness effect.
agent_relevance: Fixation can be induced by the agent's own earlier use of a tool within a session. Context carry-over inside a long run can create it.

source: Wikipedia: Functional fixedness (German and Barrett 2005, Shuar)
finding: Cross-cultural test. Shuar hunter-horticulturalists were compared with an industrial control group.
numbers: Box task: Shuar slower to select materials, same total time. Spoon task: Shuar slower in both selection and completion. Shuar were faster when artifacts were used without priming than when design function was explained. No N on the page.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Called 'preliminary'. Original Psychological Science 16:1-5 not opened.
agent_relevance: Fixation arises from learned design function. It is a property of knowledge, not of a bad mind. More knowledge of function means more fixation risk.

source: Wikipedia: Functional fixedness (McCaffrey 2012, generic parts technique)
finding: A trained technique cuts fixation. Ask of each part whether its description implies a use. If it does, make the description more generic. Candle example: wick, string, interwoven fibrous strands.
numbers: Trained participants solved 67% more problems with functional fixedness than controls. Psychological Science 23(3):215-218. No N on the page.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. No independent replication cited on the page. 67% is a relative gain.
agent_relevance: Direct template for O6: rename each object by its material and parts, not its role. This is fixation as 'failure to name' made operational.

source: Wikipedia: Einstellung effect (Luchins 1942 and later work)
finding: Luchins' water-jar problems: after several problems solved by one long method, people keep using it when a simpler method exists, and fail when it stops working.
numbers: Most experimental subjects used the long method; virtually all controls used the simple one. Failure on the extinction problem: 58% no stress vs 97% with stress. Rigidity on test problems: 70% vs 98%. Failure by age: 29% middle-aged, 65% older. Einstellung on extinction task: 56% young adults, 68% children, 69% older adults. Maze tracing: 71% normal vs 89% mirror.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. No N and no exact figure for the 1942 main result. The Ross (1952) source is not opened.
agent_relevance: Set is strengthened by repetition and by pressure. Stress raised rigidity sharply. A tight budget in a scaffold may raise fixation.

source: Wikipedia: Einstellung effect (stuttering study)
finding: Einstellung varies with person state. Stutterers showed more set effect on a hidden-word task.
numbers: 58% of stutterers vs 4% of fluent speakers used the Einstellung solution on the first two critical problems.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Small special sample. Not a general result.
agent_relevance: Set strength depends on the solver's condition. For a model, the 'condition' may be context length and prior tokens.

source: Wikipedia: Wolfgang Kohler (Tenerife apes; The Mentality of Apes 1917)
finding: Kohler studied chimpanzees on Tenerife from 1913 and published in 1917. Apes stacked crates and used sticks to reach bananas. He read this as insight and set it against Thorndike's trial and error.
numbers: Most observations in the first six months of 1914. Six years at the station. The page gives no counts of apes, trials or latencies.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Later critics (not on the page) argue that prior experience explains much of the apes' success. Not opened here.
agent_relevance: Insight is defined by a sudden change in how the situation is seen, after a stuck phase. This is the pattern S6 and O6 should detect.

source: Wikipedia: Insight (Gestalt origins and findings)
finding: Insight was first studied by Gestalt psychologists as an alternative to associationism. Metcalfe's warmth ratings: people predict progress well on non-insight problems and poorly on insight problems.
numbers: Incubation: a 4-minute break helped as much as 12 minutes. Sleep: sleepers did about twice as well as those awake. EEG: alpha/gamma activity about 300 ms before insight solutions. Survey: almost 20% of Australian respondents report never having an insight.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. No sample sizes.
agent_relevance: Sudden jumps are not predicted by the solver's own progress estimate. A model's self-reported confidence cannot detect impasse; code-side signals must.

source: Wikipedia: Gestalt psychology (productive vs reproductive thinking)
finding: Wertheimer split thinking into productive (insight, structure-driven) and reproductive (past experience, algorithm, trial and error). Duncker coined functional fixedness. Wertheimer's Productive Thinking appeared in 1945.
numbers: Page gives no experimental numbers for these. Criticism: vague terms like Pragnanz, weak testable neural models, little quantitative work.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Only the first 100,000 of 130,872 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Gives the founding contrast our scaffold needs: reproduction (retrieve a known method) vs production (restructure). Fixation is reproduction applied where restructuring is needed.

source: Wikipedia: Karl Duncker
finding: Duncker (1903-1940) published Zur Psychologie des produktiven Denkens (1935); English On Problem Solving (1945, Psychological Monographs 58). He coined functional fixedness and posed the X-ray (tumor) problem.
numbers: Exiled 1935; Swarthmore. Died aged 37. The page gives no results for the radiation problem.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Radiation problem figures not on the page.
agent_relevance: Duncker's account: solutions emerge by successive reformulation of the goal. This matches a reframe operator that restates the goal one level up.

source: Wikipedia: Nine-dot problem
finding: Classic 'think outside the box' problem. Solution needs lines to go outside the dot square. Used to study insight.
numbers: Four lines through a 3x3 grid. Printed 1907 (Pearson). General n x n needs 2n-2 segments (Klamkin 1955; Selfridge 1956).
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. No hint-effect numbers (Weisberg and Alba 1981 etc.).
agent_relevance: The fixation here is an implicit constraint the solver invented (stay inside the square). Operator: list assumed constraints and test which are in the task text.

source: Wikipedia: Mental set
finding: Functional fixedness is a special case of rigidity. Mental set is studied through problem solving and anagrams; set-shifting links to working memory and inhibitory control. Rokeach (1948) linked water-jar rigidity to ethnocentrism.
numbers: No effect sizes. Kteily and Brandt (2025): link of political ideology to rigidity is small and measure-dependent.
limits: Wikipedia (secondary); primary paper not opened. Does not discuss Einstellung studies or replications.
agent_relevance: Set-shifting is tied to inhibition and working memory in people. Model analogue: an instruction to inhibit the first-found method must be explicit and checked.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: First LLM benchmark built for fixation/Einstellung. 618 Only Connect walls: 16 clues, 4 groups of 4, with deliberate red herrings. Test set 494 walls. None of static embeddings, PLMs or LLMs solved the task at human level.
numbers: Human expert baseline on test set: 285 of 494 walls solved, 1405 of 1976 groups. GPT-4 few-shot: 3 to 7 walls solved, 239 to 272 groups. GPT-3.5: 0-2 walls, 114-149 groups.
quote: Surprisingly, more in-context examples (from 1 to 10 shot) did not improve performance.
limits: Quiz-show experts are a strong human baseline. Many clues need niche cultural knowledge, so low scores are not only fixation. Only 2023 models tested.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable fixation proxy: how much a model loses when decoys are present. Useful as a test bench for O6.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) red-herring ablation (OCW-Randomized, OCW-WordNet)
finding: Removing red herrings greatly raises LLM scores. This supports the claim that decoy groups, not task knowledge alone, cause the failures.
numbers: Walls solved (of 494) at 0/1/3/5/10-shot. GPT-4 original OCW: 6, 4, 5, 7, 3. GPT-4 OCW-Randomized: 59, 57, 62, 68, 55. GPT-4 OCW-WordNet: 471, 304, 279, 298, 378. GPT-3.5 original 0-2; Randomized 5-17; WordNet 337-428.
limits: Table column order read from a plain-text extraction of the PDF; the GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 split is inferred from row order. Randomized walls change difficulty in other ways than red herrings alone. WordNet walls are a different task type. Causal claim is plausible, not isolated.
agent_relevance: Roughly a 10-fold rise in solved walls (about 5 to about 60) from removing decoys. The cost of a tempting wrong frame is large for models too.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Task 2 connections and error profile
finding: Naming the connection of a given group is easier than finding the group, but still well below humans.
numbers: Human: about 80% of connections correct. GPT-4 10-shot ROUGE-1/BERTScore F1 about 41-45%. Exact match under 15%. Task 1 error sources for GPT-4 3-shot: misformatted groups 4.4%, hallucinated clues 6.6%. Connections that wrongly included clues: 8.2%.
limits: F1 vs human percent-correct is not like for like, as the paper says.
agent_relevance: Weak point is the grouping step (choosing a frame), not the naming step.

source: Tian et al. (2023/2025) MacGyver: Are LLMs creative problem solvers?
finding: Dataset of over 1,600 real-world problems built to need unconventional object use (functional fixedness). Over 82% of solvable problems need tools used in non-standard ways. Built by progressive refinement: add constraints that remove the obvious solution, add distractor objects.
numbers: 1,306 problems judged solvable (77.6%), 377 unsolvable (22.4%). A 323-problem sample was given to 7 LLMs and to N=252 UK Prolific participants (about 6 responses per problem).
limits: Human judges were MTurk US raters. Dataset is machine generated then human screened. Text only, so no physical feedback.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of functional fixedness in LLMs. Design idea: make the obvious tool use impossible and see whether the agent finds the other use.

source: Tian et al. MacGyver: LLM vs human accuracy
finding: Most LLMs get a third to two-fifths of problems right. Humans do better on average. Humans have higher variance; GPT-4 is more even.
numbers: LLM success 35-42% (single attempt). Average person: total correct 65.1%. Multi-effort comparison: majority of humans 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%. Best of four humans: near perfect. Scale alone gave no clear gain (Llama2 7b/13b/70b).
limits: Success counts correct solutions plus correct unsolvable calls; the mix differs by model. PaLM2 and GPT-4 over-answer unsolvable items; Llama2-7b, Claude2, GPT-3.5 over-refuse.
agent_relevance: Two failure types: propose-anything (verbose) and refuse (conservative). The agent needs a feasibility check, not only a creative generator.

source: Tian et al. MacGyver: GPT-4 error analysis
finding: Manual analysis of 200 GPT-4 solutions judged infeasible. The largest cause is physically wrong tool use, not rigidity of the usual kind.
numbers: Wrong tool usage 42.4%; fails to achieve goal 17.7%; using unavailable tools 16.9%; unfaithful to constraints 9.5% (the two hallucination types together 26.4%).
limits: Percent split of efficient/inefficient/infeasible outcomes was in a garbled figure layer and is not reported here.
agent_relevance: LLM 'fixation' looks like wrong affordance modelling more than stuck-on-the-usual-use. S1 diagnosis should check physical or logical feasibility of each reuse.

source: Tian et al. MacGyver: prompting fixes (self-reflect, divergent-convergent)
finding: Two prompts: iterative step-wise reflection, and divergent-convergent thinking (list every object's affordances first, then converge on a plan). Tested on 180 solvable problems with GPT-4, Claude2, Llama2-13b.
numbers: GPT-4: self-reflect cut infeasible solutions by 9.7 points (div-conv 4.3). Div-conv raised efficient solutions by 6.5 points (self-reflect 2.2). Div-conv helped all three models. Self-reflect did not help Claude2 or Llama2-13b, which changed answers blindly.
limits: Gains are single-digit points on 180 items, no confidence intervals. One dataset.
agent_relevance: Supports O6 as 'enumerate affordances first' (divergent step) before any plan. Reflection without real output (G2) is unreliable in smaller models.

source: Liu, Karimnazarov and White (2025) Trapped by Expectations: functional fixedness in LLM chat search
finding: Functional fixedness in human users of an LLM tool. Prior experience with ChatGPT, search engines or assistants shapes how people prompt, and limits what they try.
numbers: 450 crowd participants, 6 decision-making tasks, multi-prompt ChatGPT conversations. Virtual-assistant users wrote directive, command-like prompts. Search users wrote structured queries. Unmet expectations led to longer, more varied prompts. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: About human fixation on the tool, not model fixation. Abstract only; full text not read.
agent_relevance: Fixation also sits on the user side: the scaffold should not assume users know to ask for a reframe.

source: CresOWLve (2026) Benchmarking creative problem-solving over real-world knowledge
finding: Benchmark of puzzles needing lateral links across facts. Models retrieve the facts but fail to form the non-obvious connection.
numbers: 2,061 examples, 5 difficulty levels. Accuracy drops by up to 17% on creative vs factual questions. COLM 2026. Models not named in the abstract.
limits: Authors and model list not read; abstract only. Does not mention fixation by name.
agent_relevance: Matches the S1/O6 gap: the knowledge is there, the frame is not. Retrieval of facts does not solve reframing.

source: Beda and Smith (2018) Chasing red herrings (as cited in Naeini et al. 2023)
finding: Fixation in the Remote Associates Test comes from memory strength of the misleading clue. Repetition and context raise it.
numbers: Naeini et al. cite it for the corollary that memory strength of red herrings sets fixation size. No numbers in the citing paper.
limits: Read only as cited. Original (Memory and Cognition 46:671-684) not opened.
agent_relevance: Fixation scales with how strongly the decoy is retrieved. An agent that has written a wrong frame at length has strengthened it; a fresh context may reduce it.

source: Duncker (1945) On problem solving (recalled, not opened)
finding: Candle/box, pliers and other 'functional fixedness' tasks. Duncker also described solving as repeated reformulation of the goal, from general solution to functional value to specific form.
numbers: Exact counts not retrieved this session.
limits: NOT OPENED. Background only; confirm before use.
agent_relevance: Reformulating the goal in steps is the Gestalt prototype of operator O6.

source: Luchins (1942) Mechanization in problem solving (recalled, not opened)
finding: Water-jar set effect: a trained rule is applied even when a shorter one exists.
numbers: Exact group N and percentages not retrieved; Wikipedia says only 'most' vs 'virtually all'.
limits: NOT OPENED. Verify effect size before quoting.
agent_relevance: Repeated success with one method hardens it. Ban the last method as a test, only when a check fails (G1).

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones (recalled, not opened)
finding: Chess experts who had found a familiar winning line believed they searched for a better one, but eye tracking showed gaze stayed on the familiar line.
numbers: Exact N and Elo drop not retrieved. Do not cite numbers.
limits: NOT OPENED. Recollection only.
agent_relevance: Reported search is not real search. The agent's stated 'I considered alternatives' is not evidence; code must check that a new frame was actually tried (G2).

source: Weisberg and Alba (1981) nine-dot hints (recalled, not opened)
finding: Telling people to go outside the dot square gave little help; many still failed. Argued the block is not only the assumed boundary.
numbers: Exact percentages not retrieved.
limits: NOT OPENED. Usual counter to a pure fixed-assumption story; progress monitoring (MacGregor, Ormerod, Chronicle 2001) is a rival account.
agent_relevance: A hint to reframe is not enough alone. A scaffold must also supply the concrete new move.
